app.title: Trust Lab
app.tagline: An interactive guide to why strangers cooperate

outcome.CC: You both shared. Each of you gets {you}.
outcome.CD: You shared, they kept. You get {you}, they get {them}.
outcome.DC: You kept, they shared. You get {you}, they get {them}.
outcome.DD: You both kept. Each of you gets {you}.

alwaysCooperate.name: Dove
alwaysCooperate.desc: Shares every single time, no matter what.

alwaysDefect.name: Shark
alwaysDefect.desc: Never shares. Takes whatever it can get.

titForTat.name: Monkey
titForTat.desc: Shares first, then does whatever you did last round.

grimTrigger.name: Elephant
grimTrigger.desc: Shares until you betray it once. After that it never forgets and never shares again.

pavlov.name: Dog
pavlov.desc: Shares first. If you both made the same choice last round it shares, otherwise it keeps.

titForTwoTats.name: Tortoise
titForTwoTats.desc: Very patient. Only hits back after you betray it twice in a row.

prober.name: Fox
prober.desc: Cunning. Tests you with Keep, Share, Share. If you hit back, it plays fair like the Monkey. If not, it exploits you.

status.notDilemma: With these payoffs it is no longer a real dilemma.

home.title: Why do strangers trust each other?
home.lead: Every day, people cooperate with others they barely know, even when cheating would pay more in the moment. In this lab you will play a simple trading game, pit strategies against each other and watch whole populations evolve.
home.hint: Point at or tap a character to hear how it plays.

rules.title: The deal
rules.intro: Two traders meet at a market stall. Each one secretly decides to Share or Keep. Then both choices are revealed at the same time and points are handed out.
rules.tryIt: Sit down at the table. You play the Monkey; across from you is the Fox. Each click is one round — play a few and watch what the Fox does.

table.label: The trading table with both revealed choices

trap.title: The trap
trap.body: Whatever the other trader does, keeping earns you more: {temptation} instead of {reward} if they share, {punishment} instead of {sucker} if they keep. But if both of you follow that logic, you each walk away with {punishment} instead of {reward}.
trap.question: So is sharing just naive? Let’s find out.

play.title: Your turn
play.intro: You will trade with five strangers, one after another. Each has their own way of playing. You won’t know how many rounds a meeting lasts, just like in real life.

match.over: The stranger packs up and leaves.

reveal.title: Who were they?
reveal.total: Your total: {n} point | Your total: {n} points
reveal.hint: Look at who you could build trust with, and who simply took advantage of you.

tournament.title: The tournament
tournament.intro: Let’s step back and let the strategies play each other. Every participant meets every other participant for one match. Points from all matches are added up.
tournament.insight: Strategies that start nice but hit back when cheated usually finish near the top. But the ranking depends on who else is in the room. Try removing a few participants, or set the match length to 1 round.

evolution.title: Generations
evolution.intro: Markets change. After every tournament, the lowest scorers leave and the top scorers each bring along a newcomer who plays just like them. What spreads over time?

doves.title: Doves and Sharks
doves.desc: Lots of trusting Doves, a few Sharks and a few Monkeys. The Sharks feast first. Who has the last word?

oneShot.title: One-time meetings
oneShot.desc: The same crowd, but every pair meets only once. Without a future, does trust survive?

everyone.title: Everyone together
everyone.desc: Three of every strategy. Who takes over the market?

mistakes.title: When mistakes happen
mistakes.intro: So far everyone did exactly what they intended. Real life is messier: a delivery gets lost, a message is misread. Here every move has a chance to come out wrong.
mistakes.lesson: A little forgiveness helps trust survive accidents. Too much forgiveness invites exploiters.

clean.title: No mistakes
clean.desc: Monkeys, Elephants, Dogs and Tortoises live together, with one Shark in the mix.

noisy.title: 10% mistakes
noisy.desc: The same population, but one move in ten goes wrong. A single accident can start an endless feud between two Monkeys, and an Elephant never forgives.

sandbox.title: Sandbox
sandbox.intro: Now it’s your world. Change the population, the length of meetings, the chance of mistakes and even the payoffs. Can you build a world where trust wins? Or one where it collapses?

end.title: What we learned
end.closing: None of this asks you to be naive. Start kind, respond fairly and leave room for second chances.
end.credits: Built on decades of game theory research, especially Robert Axelrod’s computer tournaments, and inspired by Nicky Case’s “The Evolution of Trust”.

future.title: Trust needs a future
future.body: When people expect to meet again, sharing pays off. When every meeting is a one-off, keeping wins.

winwin.title: Both sides must gain
winwin.body: If sharing pays too little, or cheating pays too much, trust collapses. Try it in the sandbox.

forgive.title: Mistakes call for forgiveness
forgive.body: In a noisy world, strategies that hit back but also forgive do better than those that hold grudges.

kids.title: Game theory games for kids
kids.lead: 25 games built on classic game theory ideas, made for kids. Just cookies, chores, recess and a lot of “I think that you think that I think…”.
kids.intro: Game theory is about how your best move depends on what other people do. Its famous puzzles usually come from the grown-up world: markets, prices, rules and contests. Here each idea moves into a kid’s world (the classroom, the playground, the kitchen, the lemonade stand) but keeps the same lesson. Most games need only paper, pencils, a die and some sweets or tokens.

tictactoe.title: Tic-Tac-Toe Detective
tictactoe.source: Thinking ahead: noughts and crosses as a mini chess
tictactoe.step1: Play 5 normal games and count the wins.
tictactoe.step2: New rule: before every move, say out loud: “If I go here, you’ll go there.”
tictactoe.step3: Play 5 more games and count the draws.
tictactoe.idea: Once both players think one move ahead, nobody wins. That is why chess masters draw so often.
tictactoe.ask: Why did the games get “boring” once you both got good?

magicNumber.title: The Two-Thirds Magic Number
magicNumber.step1: Everyone secretly writes a number from 0 to 100.
magicNumber.step2: The teacher works out the average and takes two-thirds of it (younger kids can use half).
magicNumber.step3: The closest guess wins a sticker.
magicNumber.step4: Play again and watch the numbers shrink every round!
magicNumber.idea: Smart players think about what others will guess. If everyone thought that way forever, the answer would be 0, but real people stop sooner.
magicNumber.ask: In the real newspaper contest the winning number was 13. Why not 0?

classFavourite.title: Guess the Class Favourite
classFavourite.step2: Don’t vote for your own favourite. Vote for the one you think most of the class will pick.
classFavourite.step3: Everyone who picked the winner scores a point.
classFavourite.idea: Sometimes winning means guessing what the crowd thinks, not what you like.
classFavourite.ask: Did you pick your real favourite? Why not?

lemonade.title: Lemonade Stand Weekend
lemonade.source: Two rivals picking a day, and Nash equilibrium
lemonade.step1: Two lemonade stands each secretly pick Saturday (more people out) or Sunday.
lemonade.step2: Reveal and score with the grid. On the same day you share the customers.
lemonade.step3: Circle each player’s best answer to each choice. The box with two circles is the spot nobody regrets.
lemonade.idea: A Nash equilibrium is a spot where nobody wishes they had chosen differently.
lemonade.ask: Would either stand want to switch days once they see the result?

gameTree.title: Choose-Your-Path Game Tree
gameTree.source: Taking turns: sequential games and game trees
gameTree.step1: Two best friends want to hang out. One loves the pool, the other loves the skate park.
gameTree.step2: Player 1 goes first and texts “I’m at the pool!”. Then Player 2 chooses.
gameTree.step3: Draw it as a tree: the first branch belongs to Player 1, the next branches to Player 2.
gameTree.step4: Start at the bottom leaves and work backwards to find the best first move.
gameTree.idea: Going first can be a superpower: your friend follows you because being together beats being alone.
gameTree.ask: Would it be better to go first or second? Why?

threats.title: “I’ll Never Speak to You Again!”
threats.step1: Read threat cards aloud, for example: “If you go to the pool, I’ll stay home alone all day!”
threats.step2: The group votes: believe it or bluff?
threats.step3: Test it: when the moment comes, would carrying out the threat hurt the person who made it?
threats.idea: A threat only works if carrying it out is still the best move when the time comes.
threats.ask: Can you think of a threat you once heard that was really a bluff?

tripVote.title: The Class Trip Vote Loop
tripVote.source: Group decisions and Arrow’s Impossibility Theorem
tripVote.step1: Three council members get secret ranking cards for the zoo, the pool and the museum. A: zoo, pool, museum. B: pool, museum, zoo. C: museum, zoo, pool.
tripVote.step2: Vote two at a time: zoo against pool, then the winner against the museum.
tripVote.step3: Now vote the first loser against the final winner. Surprise!
tripVote.idea: Everyone is sensible, yet the group goes round in circles. Whoever picks the voting order picks the winner.
tripVote.ask: Is there a fair way to decide? Who should choose the order?

cookie.title: Share or Grab: The Cookie Dilemma
cookie.step1: Each player secretly shows a Share or a Grab card.
cookie.step2: Both share: 3 cookies each. Both grab: 1 each. One grabs and one shares: the grabber gets 5, the sharer 0.
cookie.idea: Grabbing always looks smarter for you alone, but when you both grab, you both lose out.
cookie.ask: What would make it easier to trust each other?

tournament.title: Friendship Tournament
tournament.step1: Play the Cookie Dilemma again and again with the same partner.
tournament.step2: After each round roll a die. A 6 ends the match, so nobody knows which round is the last.
tournament.step3: Try out personalities: always nice, copycat (do what they did last time), never forgive.
tournament.step4: Then play exactly 5 rounds that everyone knows about. What happens in round 5?
tournament.idea: When you will meet again, being kind pays. When everyone knows it is the last round, trust falls apart.
tournament.ask: Which personality did best? Was it the nicest one?

toyRoom.title: Who Tidies the Toy Room?
toyRoom.step1: Each sibling secretly picks Tidy or Chill. Both chill: 10 each. You chill while they tidy: 20 for you, 8 for them. Both tidy: 14 each.
toyRoom.step2: Round 2: add a guilty-feeling card. Choosing Chill now costs 7 points.
toyRoom.step3: Compare what happens with and without the guilty feeling.
toyRoom.idea: Good habits and feeling responsible change the scores, so teamwork becomes the smart move.
toyRoom.ask: Who tidies up at your home, and why?

fishPond.title: The Magic Fish Pond
fishPond.source: The tragedy of the commons and environmental cooperation
fishPond.step1: The pond (the bowl) starts with 20 fish (sweets).
fishPond.step2: Each round, every player secretly decides how many fish to catch: 0 to 3.
fishPond.step3: After the catch, the fish left in the pond double, up to 20.
fishPond.step4: If the pond is ever empty, the game is over for everyone.
fishPond.idea: Shared things get used up when everyone takes “just a little extra”. That is why the planet needs agreements.
fishPond.ask: What rule would keep the pond full forever?

whisper.title: Library Whisper Battle
whisper.source: A shared channel where everyone turns up the volume
whisper.step1: Two teams each pass secret words to a partner across the room at the same time.
whisper.step2: Each team chooses: whisper or shout.
whisper.step3: Count the words that got through in 30 seconds. A shouting team drowns out a whispering one, and two shouting teams drown each other out.
whisper.idea: Radios and phones share the airwaves too! That is why there are rules that make devices take turns and keep the volume down.
whisper.ask: Where else does everyone end up shouting?
whisper.concept: A winning move that hurts everyone

iceCream.title: Two Ice-Cream Vans, One Tiny Town
iceCream.step1: The town only has enough kids for one ice-cream van.
iceCream.step2: Each day both vans secretly choose Stay or Leave.
iceCream.step3: Both stay: each loses 2 tokens. Only one stays: it earns 8. A van that leaves gets 0 and is out.
iceCream.step4: Keep going until someone leaves. Did the fight cost more than the prize?
iceCream.idea: Stubborn contests can cost more than the thing you are fighting over.
iceCream.ask: When is it smart to give up first?

movieOrPark.title: Cinema or Park? (No Phones!)
movieOrPark.step1: Two friends want to meet. One prefers the cinema, the other the park, but being together beats everything.
movieOrPark.step2: Without talking, each secretly writes where they will go.
movieOrPark.step3: Together at your favourite: 10. Together at theirs: 5. Apart: 0.
movieOrPark.step4: Round 2: the teacher first plays a “radio ad” for one place. Does that help?
movieOrPark.idea: When there are several good answers, hints, habits and ads help everyone land on the same one.
movieOrPark.ask: How do you and your friends decide without talking?

meetMe.title: Meet Me Somewhere!
meetMe.source: Thomas Schelling and meeting points everyone thinks of
meetMe.step1: “You lost your friend at school and can’t call. Where and when do you go to find them?”
meetMe.step2: Everyone secretly writes a place and a time.
meetMe.step3: Score a point for every classmate who wrote the same thing.
meetMe.idea: Some answers stand out for everyone, like the main gate at noon. Shared habits help us coordinate.
meetMe.ask: Why did so many people pick the same place?

piggyBank.title: Piggy-Bank Panic
piggyBank.step1: Everyone deposits 5 marbles in the class bank. The bank “lends” most of them (puts them aside) and keeps only 10.
piggyBank.step2: If you wait until the end, you get your 5 back plus 1 bonus marble.
piggyBank.step3: Each round anyone can run up and withdraw: first come, first served, until the 10 run out!
piggyBank.step4: Whisper a rumour: “I heard the bank is in trouble…” and watch what happens.
piggyBank.idea: If everyone believes the bank will run out, it really will. The worry itself causes the problem.
piggyBank.ask: What could the bank do to calm everyone down?
piggyBank.concept: Fears that make themselves come true

rps.title: Rock-Paper-Scissors Pattern Hunter
rps.step1: Player A gets a secret card: “Throw rock a lot!” (8 times out of 10).
rps.step2: Player B tallies A’s throws and tries to spot the pattern.
rps.step3: Swap roles. Now A rolls a die to choose: 1–2 rock, 3–4 paper, 5–6 scissors. Can B still win?
rps.idea: If you are predictable, you can be beaten. Being truly random, a third of the time each, cannot be beaten on average.
rps.ask: How long did it take to spot the pattern?

goats.title: Two Goats on a Narrow Bridge
goats.step1: Two goats meet on a one-goat bridge. Each secretly picks Push On or Step Back.
goats.step2: One pushes on and one steps back: the pusher gets 5, the other 1. Both step back: 2 each. Both push: splash! Both fall in the river and lose 5.
goats.step3: Play 10 rounds. How often did you splash?
goats.idea: Both want to be the brave one. If you mix it up, a splash sometimes happens.
goats.ask: Is it braver to push on or to step back?

homework.title: Surprise Homework Check
homework.step1: Students secretly choose Do homework (costs 2 points of fun) or Skip.
homework.step2: The teacher secretly chooses Check (costs the teacher 1 point) or Don’t check.
homework.step3: Caught skipping: minus 5. The teacher earns 3 for every skipper caught.
homework.step4: After many rounds: how often should the teacher check?
homework.idea: If the teacher always checks, nobody skips, so checking is wasted. If they never check, everyone skips. The answer is a surprising mix!
homework.ask: Would you skip if you knew the teacher checks only sometimes?

sandcastle.title: Sneak Attack on the Sandcastle
sandcastle.step1: The Wave secretly picks one day from 1 to 7 to crash into the castle.
sandcastle.step2: The Builder secretly picks one day to build a wall.
sandcastle.step3: If the Builder guesses the day, the castle is safe. Otherwise the Wave wins.
sandcastle.step4: Repeat. The Wave quickly learns to pick truly at random.
sandcastle.idea: Surprise is the whole point. A predictable attack gets blocked.
sandcastle.ask: Which days did the Wave pick most often? Did the Builder notice?

hawkDove.title: Hawks and Doves at the Bird Feeder
hawkDove.source: The Hawk-Dove Game and evolutionary stability
hawkDove.step1: Each kid wears a hawk or a dove badge. Pair up randomly at the feeder (20 seeds).
hawkDove.step2: Hawk against dove: the hawk takes everything. Dove against dove: share. Hawk against hawk: fight! Flip a coin; the loser gets hurt and loses 24.
hawkDove.step3: After each round the lowest scorers switch to the type that did better (“babies copy the winners”).
hawkDove.step4: Write the number of hawks on the board after every round.
hawkDove.idea: When fights are costly, nature finds a balance: a mix of hawks and doves, here about 5 hawks for every dove.
hawkDove.ask: Why didn’t the hawks take over completely?

bike.title: Borrow My Bike?
bike.step1: Kid A wants to borrow Kid B’s bike and promises: “I’ll ride carefully!”
bike.step2: Once A has the bike, A can ride carefully (1 point of fun) or do jumps (5 points, but the bike might break).
bike.step3: Should B lend it? Draw the tree.
bike.step4: Now A leaves their favourite toy as a pledge. Does that change everything?
bike.idea: Promises are easier to believe when you have something to lose if you break them.
bike.ask: What else could A offer so that B believes the promise?

cardSwap.title: Mystery Card Swap
cardSwap.step1: Sellers get sealed envelopes with a shiny card (worth 6) or a dud (worth 1). Only the seller can peek.
cardSwap.step2: Buyers offer tokens for an envelope without seeing inside.
cardSwap.step3: Watch: buyers offer little because they fear duds, so owners of shiny cards refuse to sell.
cardSwap.idea: When only one side knows the truth, good things can disappear from the market.
cardSwap.ask: How could a seller prove that their card is really shiny?

lemonadePromise.title: Prove It! The Lemonade Promise
lemonadePromise.source: Signals: warranties, free samples and adverts
lemonadePromise.step1: Each stand secretly draws Tasty or Sour lemonade.
lemonadePromise.step2: Shouting “Ours is the best!” is free, so everyone does it and nobody believes it.
lemonadePromise.step3: Now stands can offer “Money back if you don’t love it!”. Each refund costs the stand 2 tokens.
lemonadePromise.step4: Which stands dare to make the promise? What do customers learn?
lemonadePromise.idea: Talk is cheap. A promise that would be too expensive for a bad product tells you something true.
lemonadePromise.ask: Where have you seen a promise like that in real shops?

teamLoan.title: Team Loan Challenge
teamLoan.step1: The bank lends each kid 3 tokens to “start a business”, a quick mini-game such as throwing a bean bag.
teamLoan.step2: The catch: if anyone in your trio can’t pay back, nobody in the trio gets a loan next round.
teamLoan.step3: Watch how the teams help and remind each other.
teamLoan.idea: When your friends’ success is tied to yours, you look out for each other, and a bank can trust people who have no money.
teamLoan.ask: Did your team help the weakest player? How?

map.title: From big ideas to the playground

skipped.title: Topics left out for this age
skipped.nuclear: Nuclear deterrence and the doomsday machine: too frightening for this age. The idea of believable threats lives on in “I’ll Never Speak to You Again!”.
skipped.work: Wages, unemployment and lazy workers: the workplace is too far from kids’ lives. Random checks live on in the Surprise Homework Check.
skipped.religion: Religious ritual as a signal: a sensitive topic. Costly signals are taught through the Lemonade Promise instead.

tips.title: Tips for grown-ups
tips.playFirst: Play first, explain later. Let kids feel the surprise (“we both grabbed and both lost!”) before you name the idea.
tips.rewards: Use small real rewards. Stickers or single sweets make choices feel real without hurt feelings.
tips.debrief: Always talk it over afterwards: “What would you do differently?” and “Where have you seen this in real life?”.
tips.path: A four-week plan: week 1 think ahead, week 2 share or grab, week 3 mind-reading and surprises, week 4 nature and trust.

kids.credits: All games are original classroom adaptations of well-known ideas from game theory.
